newsitem.title: INDONESIA: S.E. Asian cocoa producers mull common contract.
newsitem.headline: S.E. Asian cocoa producers mull common contract.

text.p: Southeast Asian cocoa producers opened a two-day meeting on Tuesday to explore setting up a regional trading contract to reduce dependence on foreign pacts.
Conference delegates said there was a long way to go before the contract, covering the seven members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), could be realised, however.
"We want to make an inventory of the very important factors for this contract," conference chairman Suharyo Husen of Indonesia's Agriculture Ministry told Reuters.
"The contract will be in the interest of all ASEAN members. We want to increase our trade...with common regulations and control (over) quality and to improve our competitiveness."
He said Indonesia would make a decision on the move after consulting with the ministries of industry and trade, agriculture and foreign affairs.
"We also need to look at the laws," he said, adding that the process would take time.

He said government and private sector representatives from Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Malaysia -- which together with Brunei and Vietnam comprise ASEAN -- were attending the meeting.
The move to set up the common contract is being spearheaded by Malaysia in a bid to bridge the quality gap among Southeast Asian cocoa producers and narrow existing price disparities.
Indonesia and Malaysia are the region's top two producers.
"We will be discussing the proposed contract at this meeting," said Mohamed Musa Jamil, head of the Malaysian Cocoa Board. "If everyone agrees, we will proceed from there."
"The project will take time to be implemented, as many things have to be put in place first," he said.
Siswoputranto, executive director of the Indonesian Cocoa Association, said Indonesia had to be cautious.

"There has been a political decision by ASEAN on the contract, and we need to fulfil it but we need to be cautious. The ASEAN contract should be an alternative to contracts in London and New York," he told reporters.
He said a common regional contract would allow independent Southeast Asian countries to avoid dependence on foreign pacts.
"When we are doing business with Vietnam, for instance, why should we be using London contracts," he said. "It is the same with other intra-ASEAN business (in cocoa).
Delegates said an ASEAN contract would offer other advantages such as providing dispute-solving mechanisms within the region.
"The problem now is whether the contract we want to set up will gain the confidence of the international cocoa community," Siswoputranto said. "That's the key."
Indonesia, the world's third largest cocoa producer after the Ivory Coast and Ghana, has been forecast to produce between 319,000 and 330,000 tonnes in 1997, up 10 percent from 1996.
Malaysia's 1997 output is expected to remain unchanged at its 1996 level of 125,00 tonnes.
